# The grammar of graphics

Before we touch the real data, let's learn the one idea that powers every plot in
`ggplot2`: the **grammar of graphics**. Every plot is built from three pieces:

> **data** → **aesthetics** (`aes`: which column goes on x, y, colour…) → **geom** (how to draw it)

We'll learn it on a tiny built-in dataset, `mpg` (fuel economy of cars), then use it
on our bacteria.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
head(mpg)
```

A plot grows by adding layers with `+`:

```{r}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +   # data + aesthetics
  geom_point()                           # geom: draw points
```

Add a **colour** aesthetic and a second **layer** (a trend line):

```{r, message=FALSE}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, colour = class)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  labs(title = "Bigger engines use more fuel",
       x = "Engine size (L)", y = "Highway mpg")
```

That's the whole idea. Everything today is just **data → aes → geom + layers**.

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Principle:</strong> pick the <em>aesthetic</em> for each variable
  (position, colour, shape…) and the <em>geom</em> for how to show it. Change those
  two and you change the plot.
</div>

### 👉 Your turn {-}

Using `mpg`, make a scatter plot of `cty` (x) vs `hwy` (y), and colour the points by
`drv` (drivetrain). Then give it proper axis labels.

<details>
<summary>Solution</summary>
```{r, eval=FALSE}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = cty, y = hwy, colour = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "City mpg", y = "Highway mpg", colour = "Drivetrain")
```
</details>

> 🤖 **Ask your AI:** *"In ggplot2, what's the difference between putting `colour =`
> inside `aes()` versus outside it?"*
